title: theDECISIONS
note: Every decision about theOS, numbered. A later decision names the one it supersedes.

decisions.title: theBRAIN is native HTML, CSS, JS and JSON
decisions.decision: Docs, wiki and architecture in theOS/theBRAIN are written as HTML, CSS, JS and JSON. No markdown.
decisions.why: One format that the app renders directly, nothing to convert, nothing to drift.

decisions.title: Agents act; humans and coops own
decisions.decision: A signer is a key that signs for an agent. Agents act; only humans and coops own data and agents.
decisions.why: Devices come and go; ownership must not move with them.

decisions.title: Three kinds of identity: human, coop, agent
decisions.decision: Identity types: human, coop, agent. Humans and coops own and decide. A coop's members are its “members” role, which holds humans or coops, never agents or signers; coops may be inside coops, never in a circle. Agents are owned and never in any role; they get policies directly from their owner.
decisions.why: Families, teams and organisations are identities of identities; one model covers all of them.

decisions.title: Data owns itself: the seal
decisions.decision: Data is born with a fresh key pair, the seal. Its public key is the data ID. It signs exactly one thing, the first policy, and the private key is wiped.
decisions.why: Nobody holds the seal, so it cannot be shared, lost or stolen. Keyhive does the same with its genesis key.

decisions.title: One owner per piece of data, and it is an identity
decisions.decision: The birth record's policy names exactly one owner: an identity, human or coop. The owner may do everything, its policy never expires, and ownership never moves to another identity (D54). The owner is not a role.
decisions.why: A role of owners cannot shrink durably: any past owner could revoke the others for good (Keyline's warning). With one owner identity, people change inside the coop, not in the data.

decisions.title: Policies go to roles, never to people directly
decisions.decision: Everyone except the owner gets access through policies. A policy is given to a role (a named set of identities) or, for an identity's own agents, to an agent directly.
decisions.why: People come and go; roles stay. Changing who is in a role never touches the data's policies.

decisions.title: People see "policies"; underneath they are capabilities
decisions.decision: The word everyone sees is "policy". Underneath, each policy is a signed capability token that carries its own proof back to the data's birth record and is checked offline.
decisions.why: "Policy" is the word ordinary people understand; capabilities are what makes it hold without a server.

decisions.title: A policy: role, data, operations, conditions, expiry, proof
decisions.decision: A policy is a signed certificate with: the role it is given to; the data it applies to; its operations, keyed by name (D56) (create, read, update, delete, want, keep, sync), each optionally narrowed by at (a path), where (matching entries) or a limit; an expiry; the signature of the owner's agent; and the proof chain back to the data's birth record. Identity policies use the same shape with act, own and govern (D48). Writing policies is not an operation: it belongs to the owner (D30).
decisions.why: One small vocabulary for content, carrying and the policies themselves. Keyhive's Relay, Read, Edit and Admin map onto it; ours is finer.

decisions.title: Sharing only narrows
decisions.decision: Whoever may share hands on a policy that is the same or smaller: fewer operations, shorter expiry, more conditions. Never more.
decisions.why: Attenuation keeps delegation safe without asking anyone. Meadowcap and Biscuit both require each step to sit inside the previous one.

decisions.title: Read is encryption, everything else is verification
decisions.decision: Opening a piece of data at all is enforced by keys; read's conditions by the reader's own engine (D55). Every other operation is enforced by every peer checking each signed change against the policies in the history.
decisions.why: Encryption can only be all or nothing per key; signature checks can be as fine as needed.

decisions.title: Reading is per piece of data; changes can be as fine as needed
decisions.decision: Read is granted per piece of data. Anything to be shared on its own is its own data. Create, update and delete can be narrowed to paths and matching entries.
decisions.why: A reader holds the plaintext, so finer read limits would be promises, not protection.

decisions.title: Every policy expires and renews itself
decisions.decision: Policies expire after 30 days unless set otherwise. The owner renews unchanged policies a week before they end, under its own policies (a coop can let one agent do renewals). The owner's first policy never expires.
decisions.why: Forgotten shares close by themselves; families are never locked out.

decisions.title: Endings: revoke and lapse
decisions.decision: A revoke (by the owner) and a lapse (by any peer that can read the policies, once the date has passed) are the same kind of event in the history. An ending wins over every change that never saw it, turns the data key if the ended policy gave read, and is the delete trigger on honest devices.
decisions.why: Validity follows from the history alone, so all copies agree. No clock is trusted.
decisions.rejected: Checking expiry against each device's own clock (copies would disagree).

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

decisions.title: Ambiguity resolves toward less authority
decisions.decision: When policy, role or ending changes are concurrent with other changes, the result with less authority wins. A change that never saw a removal or an ending is dropped (D13). Nothing wins by being “latest”: order matters only where one change has seen the other, and last-writer-wins is never used for authority (D25). When two holders remove each other at once, both removals stand and the one top repairs (D59).
decisions.why: The safe default without a central order. Keyhive's guiding principle.

decisions.title: A removed admin means a successor role
decisions.decision: When an admin is removed from a role, the role is replaced by a successor with a new ID and the remaining members are added again.
decisions.why: A removed admin can backdate a revoke by pretending not to have seen their removal. Old revokes then point at a dead role.

decisions.title: Keys: identity key, role key, data key
decisions.decision: Content is encrypted with a data key. The data key is wrapped for the owner and for each reading role. The role key is wrapped for each member's identity key. Each new data key opens the previous one, within the hot window only (D39).
decisions.why: Envelope encryption is the proven pattern (HPKE; Keybase teams, Jazz, Cryptree). Removing a member rotates one role key, not every piece of data. Forward secrecy is given up on purpose, because CRDTs need their whole history.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

decisions.title: The keyring travels with the data
decisions.decision: Each piece of data carries its keyring (envelopes, generation, back-links) next to its policies, sealed. An envelope is addressed either to a lock or to another data key (a Value bound to its metadata Doc).
decisions.why: No one keeps keys for the data; it is self-contained wherever it goes.

decisions.title: Which key turns when
decisions.decision: Adding a member or giving read: nothing turns. Removing a member: new role key, data keys on next write. Taking read: new data key now. An agent's device stolen: identity key and every role it is in. Concurrent rotations are both kept until the next one.
decisions.why: Only read touches keys; the rest is signed policies.

decisions.title: Envelopes only for published, signed locks
decisions.decision: Each agent publishes its own lock (encryption key) in its own history, signed by its signer. Envelopes are made only for locks found there, and only by someone a policy allows.
decisions.why: Stops an attacker from slipping in a lock of their own. Closes the gap Keyhive lists as G2.

decisions.title: BeeKEM inside large roles, later
decisions.decision: Small roles use one envelope per member. Roles of several dozen members and up manage their role key with BeeKEM. Not per piece of data.
decisions.why: BeeKEM per document (Keyhive) costs one update per document a removed reader could read; per role it costs one. Every Keyhive crate is pre-alpha and unaudited: pin and audit before use.

decisions.title: Data is a Doc or a Value
decisions.decision: A Doc is JSON that changes, made of CRDT data types (Loro underneath). A Value is bytes that never change, named by their BLAKE3 hash, streamed in checked ranges. Every Value has a small metadata Doc; the Value's keyring holds one envelope, addressed to that Doc's data key, so read on the Doc means read on the Value.
decisions.why: Mergeable structure where it helps, plain files where it does not.

decisions.title: Words: operation, CRDT op
decisions.decision: An operation is anything you do: what a policy allows and what the engine runs (find, update, want …). A CRDT op is Loro's low-level change, always called “CRDT op”. The slides name CRDT data types, not Loro.
decisions.why: One meaning per word.

decisions.title: The engine: JSON operations, pluggable, local
decisions.decision: Every read, change, search and sync is a JSON operation (find, walk, search, near …, and chain, which runs each step under that step's own operation). New kinds plug in and name their broad operation (D53), which a policy must allow. Operations run only on your own device, over what you can read.
decisions.why: One engine for everything, with no server in the loop.

decisions.title: Peers sync, they never ask
decisions.decision: No peer ever answers questions about its data for another peer. Peers only carry what policies allow. A shared answer is its own data with its own policy.
decisions.why: Removes the trust in the answering device, and the risk of asking one's way to the content.

decisions.title: Policies are their own signed set, not a Loro doc
decisions.decision: Policies, roles and endings are a grow-only set of signed certificates, merged by union and evaluated by our own logic.
decisions.why: Policy conflicts need "less authority wins"; Loro's last-writer-wins would resolve them wrongly. Keyhive does the same.

decisions.title: Sealed in chunks, linked by hashes
decisions.decision: Devices seal ranges of changes (Loro update bytes, compressed, then encrypted). Boundaries come from change hashes so every device cuts the same way; small chunks merge into bigger ones over time. Each chunk is hashed and lists the chunks before it; its signed header binds Loro's peer ID to the signer.
decisions.why: Sealing op by op makes data huge and uncompressible. Same lesson as Keyhive's sedimentree.

sources.label: Subduction: sync for encrypted history, with iroh transport

decisions.title: Carriers see sealed chunks and proofs, never policies
decisions.decision: Policies are sealed for readers. A carrier checks only proofs: the asker's want proof, and each change author's proof. IDs in proofs are pseudonymous.
decisions.why: Keyhive syncs its membership graph to servers in plain text; we keep that private too.

decisions.title: Peer to peer over iroh
decisions.decision: Devices connect directly over iroh: the address is the agent's signer key (D31), relays see only sealed traffic.
decisions.why: No cloud in the middle; the address can change without touching the identity.

decisions.title: Evaluate Subduction for sync
decisions.decision: Test Ink & Switch's Subduction (iroh transport, sedimentree, fingerprint sync) before building our own sync.
decisions.why: It already syncs encrypted history between peers that cannot read it. Note: current Subduction compares 8-byte fingerprints; RIBLT was in its predecessor Beelay.

sources.label: Subduction: sync for encrypted history, with iroh transport

decisions.title: Only the owner changes policies
decisions.decision: The owner writes and ends all policies on its data; ownership acts (retain, erase, open the archive, migrate to a new schema version) stay with the owner alone. Nobody else writes policies, and ownership is never handed over (D54).
decisions.why: Identities work like Gnosis Safes: agents of its members sign under the identity's own policies (one signature for now, D49), with one guardian at the top of a coop (D59). So one owner covers several managers, and there is no removed admin who could backdate a revoke.
decisions.supersedes: D15; removes admin from the role do-list in D8

decisions.title: A signer is the key of an agent
decisions.decision: A signer is only a key: the current key of exactly one agent identity, registered in that agent's history. How it is kept is up to the device the agent runs on: derived from the passkey's PRF plus a per-device salt on phones, the keychain on laptops, an environment variable, secret manager or HSM on servers. Loro's peer ID stays a number, bound to the signer in each chunk's signed header.
decisions.why: Separates who acts (identities) from what signs (keys). Not derived from the passkey alone: synced passkeys give several devices the same secret, and Apple's Secure Enclave holds only P-256 keys.
decisions.supersedes: the separate iroh key in D28

decisions.title: Words, and dialing identities
decisions.decision: Agents sign for the identity that owns them; a coop's members are its “members” role; roles are sets of identities; data is acted upon. Peers dial identities: each identity publishes a signed record of its agents, each agent's history holds its current address (its signer's public key), and the connection goes to whichever agent is online.
decisions.why: One word per thing. Addressing identities keeps the address stable while signers change, like a phone number and its SIM.

decisions.title: Sealed chunks settle in layers (sedimentree)
decisions.decision: Each sealed change is hashed (BLAKE3). Its leading zero bytes give its depth; a change of depth 1 or more closes a chunk with everything since the last one at that depth. Deeper chunks hold shallower ones. Equal content gives an equal minimal hash.
decisions.why: Every peer, even one that reads nothing, cuts the same chunks; old history becomes a few big chunks; equality is one hash.

decisions.title: Fingerprints inside data, RIBLT across data
decisions.decision: Inside one piece of data, peers compare 8-byte keyed fingerprints of its layers and swap the missing sealed chunks in 1.5 round trips. Across many pieces of data, peers use RIBLT set reconciliation to find which ones differ.
decisions.why: Sedimentree keeps the count inside one piece small, so fingerprints are cheap there; across thousands, RIBLT costs about 1.5 summaries per difference, whatever the total.

sources.label: Subduction design: batch sync with fingerprints

decisions.title: Compact at stable points; newcomers get snapshots
decisions.decision: When every writer has seen a version, a device may cut there: newcomers get a snapshot plus the ops after it, never the old history. What lies before the cut is sealed under a new key; honest devices drop the old chunks and keys.
decisions.why: CRDT history keeps deleted text and needs old keys, so forward secrecy is lost. Cutting at stable points gives it back for everything before the cut, without losing any late op.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

decisions.title: Heal: keys turn regularly
decisions.decision: Role keys and data keys turn regularly, not only when someone leaves, so a stolen key soon opens nothing new (post-compromise security). Forgetting the past is D39; the archive is D40.
decisions.why: Full forward secrecy for live CRDT history is impossible: a late op may need any old state. Keyhive gave forward secrecy up; BeeKEM's κ parameter shows the trade-off. These three layers get as close as the setting allows.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

decisions.title: Lock away: older keys behind a fresh tap
decisions.decision: Current keys stay ready on the device. Older keys, needed only for scrolling far back or merging a very late CRDT op, are sealed under an archive key derived from the passkey's PRF secret. The secure hardware releases it only after a fresh tap or face scan; afterwards it is wiped from memory.
decisions.why: A thief with the device, or malware reading app storage, gets only the current keys. Limits: malware running during the tap, or a taken-over passkey sync account.

decisions.title: Signing policies are pluggable
decisions.decision: Each identity's signing policies hold one entry per action, built from kinds: threshold (k of n), weights, all-of / any-of, time lock with objection window. A policy kind is identified by the hash of its specification and is declarative data, not code. A device that does not know a kind treats the policy as not satisfied. Changing the signing policies needs the policy for that action.
decisions.why: New kinds of signing policies can be added over time without old devices ever wrongly accepting something.

decisions.title: Keys live hot, then cold, and can be erased
decisions.decision: Hot: the newest keys, linked by back-links and ready on readers' devices; they turn regularly (D36). Cold: at rotation boundaries older than the hot window, the chain is cut; older keys leave the chain and go to the owner's archive. Erased: on request, keys are shredded everywhere. Late writers from before a cut lose and get a conflict view of what was not adopted. The hot window is 30 days, equal to a policy's lifetime.
decisions.why: Back-links and an archive cannot coexist for the same keys: a stolen current key would open the whole past. Splitting by age gives heal, archive and erasure one consistent lifecycle.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

decisions.title: The archive belongs to the owner identity
decisions.decision: Cold keys are sealed to the owner's archive key, which is itself sealed to the locks of the owner's agents that hold own (for a coop: the agents of members with own, D57). Opening the archive follows the owner's own policies. The archive key is not tied to one device. A device may add a local tap as convenience, not as protection.
decisions.why: The identity owns, never a signer (D2). Ownership of the past follows the same policies as ownership of the present.

decisions.title: Words: archive and retain
decisions.decision: Archive is the normal cold storage of old keys and history. Retain is legal long-term keeping, for a set period.
decisions.why: Two different promises, two words.

decisions.title: Erase: delete, cut, shred
decisions.decision: To erase personal data from any Doc: delete it normally, cut a fresh snapshot without it under a new key, and shred the keys of every chunk before the cut on all honest devices and in the archive; carriers drop those chunks. Works on any text, with no need to plan per piece of data. The history before the cut is lost.
decisions.why: Tombstones keep no content in the live state; the content lives only in old sealed chunks, so destroying their keys erases it (crypto-shredding). Splitting personal data into its own pieces does not scale.
decisions.rejected: Personal data as separate erasable pieces of data (does not work for a text naming ten people).

decisions.title: Retain: an owner event at any time
decisions.decision: The owner can say “retain until <date>” at any time; the date can only move later. Until then, honest devices refuse cuts, shreds and erasure. A retention role names identities that keep the sealed bytes (want, keep) and may hold an envelope of the archive key. Stored as canonical CBOR, exported as JSON and PDF/A, resealed periodically under current algorithms.
decisions.why: Bookkeeping must be kept for years (in Germany 10 years for books, 8 for vouchers since 2025; check with a tax adviser), and a legal retention duty takes priority over erasure (GDPR Art. 17(3)(b)).

decisions.title: An identity's policies and data policies never overlap
decisions.decision: An identity's own policies answer who speaks for it: policies on the identity, given to its members role or its own agents, with act, own and govern; conditions may name which data an agent acts on. A piece of data's policies answer what an identity may do with it: policies on the data, given to roles, with data operations. Signature counts appear only on identity policies (D48, D49). A change is valid only if both hold. A coop is like a small DAO: members, governance, assets, nesting.
decisions.why: Agency and access are different questions; mixing them made the coop example ambiguous.

decisions.title: Canonical CBOR for everything signed or hashed
decisions.decision: Everything that is signed, hashed or stored uses canonical CBOR (RFC 8949 deterministic encoding). Everything people read is JSON or PDF/A.
decisions.why: Same data, same bytes, same hash and signature; JSON has no canonical form. CBOR carries keys, hashes and signatures as raw bytes, keeps JSON's data model, and is what WebAuthn and COSE already use.

decisions.title: Agents: owned by one human or coop, acting by its policies
decisions.decision: An agent identity (phone, laptop, watch, server, AI assistant) is owned by exactly one human or coop and acts only through policies its owner gives it: who = the agent, on what = the owner, operations act / own / govern, with conditions (which data, limits, expiry). The owner and its first agent are born together in one record signed by the agent's key. Losing a device means revoking its agent's policy.
decisions.why: Devices are owned, not members; acting on behalf is delegation by policies (D48). One genesis record removes the chicken-and-egg problem.
decisions.supersedes: the earlier “device is a member of” model

decisions.title: Policy-writing is delegated through share, narrowing only
decisions.decision: A role holding share may write policies for other roles, but only within its own operations, conditions and expiry; it may end only policies it issued itself; when its own policy ends, every policy issued under it ends too (cascade); writes by a removed delegate that never saw the ending are dropped. The owner's policies are the root and never fall this way.
decisions.why: Gives teams day-to-day delegation without the problems of admin roles: no granting more than you hold, no policy wars between delegates, no backdated revokes.

decisions.title: One policy shape, one plugin system
decisions.decision: Every policy has one shape: who, on what, operations, conditions, expiry. An identity's policies have its members role or its own agents as who and the identity itself as target, with operations act, own and govern. A piece of data's policies have a role as who and the data as target. Operations and conditions (at, where, limit …; later signature counts, D49) are plugins in one registry, each named by the hash of its specification, declarative, failing closed when unknown. Each condition plugin declares which target it may be used on, so signature conditions stay on identities (D44).
decisions.why: One language and one engine for all policies, with the separation between agency and access kept by the target.

decisions.title: One signature by default; counts come later as plugins
decisions.decision: For now, every act, own and govern of an identity needs one signature from an agent acting under the identity's policies: its own agent, or an agent of a member (1 of 1). Govern goes to the coop's one guardian (D59). Signature counts (k of n), weights and waiting times are not part of the first version; they are added later as condition plugins (D48), and devices that do not know them treat them as not satisfied.
decisions.why: Keeps the first version simple while the plugin system leaves room to grow.

decisions.title: Record conventions
decisions.decision: Every stored or sent thing is a record: {"type": <schema ref of its kind>, …fields, "after", "seq", "sig"} (D90) in canonical CBOR (shown as JSON), decoded strictly; examples omit after and seq except where they matter (D61). IDs are typed: human:, coop:, agent:, data:, role:, policy:, ending: and chunk: followed by b3: and the BLAKE3 hash of the record without its signature; value: b3: is the hash of the bytes. A #label after an ID is only for people (human:b3:q4x7…#you). A birth record (genesis) holds a random nonce or the keys it creates, so no two share an ID. A record cannot contain its own hash, so inside a birth record the identities it creates are named by kind (“this human”, “this agent”); their IDs are b3(kind ‖ record). One genesis record can create a human or coop and its first agent. A schema is pinned as its data ID, @ and the hash of the frozen version (D66): data:b3:Sc4…@b3:1f0…#todo-list. Public keys: ed25519:… (signers), x25519:… (locks). Secret keys never appear; they are named, for example datakey:house-list/3. CRDT op IDs are Loro's peer and counter (5f3a9c:41). Times are RFC 3339 in UTC. Signatures: "sig": {"by": agent ID, "key": ed25519 public key, "value": …}; every record is signed by an agent. A proof is the ordered list of record IDs from a birth record to the acting agent; examples always show a policy's proof. Record kinds: genesis, identity, role, policy, renewal, ending, envelope, keyring, change, chunk, value, meta, retain, erase, directory, proof, want, news, operation, lens, migration. Lenses and migrations have lens: and migration: IDs. Identity policies do not expire unless they say so.
decisions.why: Slides and code use the same shapes and names, so the examples are drafts of the real schema, not illustrations.

decisions.title: Only roles and policies
decisions.decision: There are no membership records. A role is a named set of identities; a policy says what a role (or an agent) may do on an identity or a piece of data. A coop's members are its “members” role; policies on the coop say what that role may do, act and own for a home's members, only act for the homes of a street; govern goes to the coop's one guardian (D59).
decisions.why: One mechanism for everything: who is in which group (roles) and what that group may do (policies).
decisions.supersedes: membership as its own record kind

decisions.title: No data without a schema
decisions.decision: Every piece of data names a schema in its genesis; a Value's metadata Doc names one for the Value and one for itself. A schema is a JSON Schema stored as a Loro Doc with its own birth record, owner and policies. Data pins an exact schema version (the hash of the schema Doc's state); moving to a new version is an owner's change. Every peer validates every change against the schema and drops what does not fit. Paths (JSON Pointer, * for any index or key) give every part of the data an address for policies and operations.
decisions.why: Typed data makes policies and operations precise and keeps every copy well-formed without a server.

decisions.title: Engine operations are specific and typed
decisions.decision: Policies name broad operations (read, create, update, delete, want, keep, sync). Engine operations are specific and each belongs to one: read → get, find, walk, search, near, count; create → create, insert; update → set, move, splice; delete → remove, delete; chain runs each step under that step's own operation. Every operation names data, schema version and path; the engine validates its input against the plugin's shape and the schema before running it.
decisions.why: Precise, checkable operations, with policies that stay short and readable.

decisions.title: Only the owner writes policies: no passing on, no hand-over yet
decisions.decision: Only the owner writes and ends policies on its data, through its own agents. No role can pass a policy on (there is no share operation), and ownership is never handed over: whoever needs to work on the data gets a policy. Delegated, narrowing-only policy-writing may come back later as its own decision.
decisions.why: One author for a piece of data's policies keeps every check simple: no cascades, no revokes by other issuers, no backdating by a removed delegate. Policies already cover everything a hand-over would.
decisions.rejected: Share with attenuation and cascading ends (D9, D47), for now.

decisions.title: Read is an operation like any other
decisions.decision: Read carries the same conditions as every other operation (at, where, limit) and covers specific engine operations (get, find, walk, search, near, count). The data key opens a whole piece of data, so read's conditions are kept by the reader's own engine on honest devices; anything that must stay unseen is its own data, with its own key. Changes are checked by every peer.
decisions.why: One query logic for every operation: a policy always says what, where and how much. Keys still mark the hard boundary of what can be opened at all.

decisions.title: One operation shape everywhere
decisions.decision: Policies write operations as one object keyed by operation name: {"read": {"at": "/items"}, "create": {"at": "/items", "limit": 20}}, defined once as a schema. Each name appears once; its value holds the conditions: at (a JSON Pointer or a list of them, default "" = the whole data or identity), where and limit, which only narrow. The engine's record (its operation record) uses the same fields for one specific operation (find, set …). An engine operation is allowed when a policy names its broad operation, its path lies under at, and where and limit hold. The Operations object is one recursive schema: on an identity policy, act's data condition maps data IDs to Operations objects, so data policies, agent scopes and engine operations share it.
decisions.why: One source of truth for what an operation is: no repeated keys, no bare names next to objects, and every example, record and check reads the same fields.

sources.label: Meadowcap (areas: path prefixes that only narrow)

decisions.title: Keys follow agents: no shared identity key
decisions.decision: There is no key shared by all of an identity's agents. Each agent has its own lock, published in its own history (D19). A data key is sealed to the role keys of the roles that may read it and to the locks of the owner's agents whose policies cover reading it; a role key is sealed to the locks of each member's agents whose policies cover reading for that member. So an agent gets exactly the keys both layers give it: the data's policies (which identity may read) and the identity's policies (which of its agents reads for it, D58). Carriers get none. Any current reader that has seen a change in the reader set may turn a key; every peer checks that envelopes go only to current readers. When two key turns are concurrent, the next key is sealed only to the readers both allowed, and nobody encrypts under a generation older than an ending it knows. Adding someone: envelopes for their reading agents; a newcomer starts from today's snapshot unless the owner opens older history. Removing someone or losing an agent: it gets nothing new, and every role key and data key it could open turns (role keys now, data keys on the next write; data keys now when read is taken).
decisions.why: Reading must follow the same delegation as writing: a watch limited to health data, or a backup with only want and keep, must not be able to decrypt everything, and removing a coop member must stop their reading without a cascade of identity-key turns. Keyhive does the same: every individual with Read is a leaf of the key tree, one with only Relay is not.

decisions.title: An agent has two parts: who it is, and what it may do
decisions.decision: An agent is its own identity, owned by exactly one human or coop, with its own signer; on phones the signer is derived from the passkey, which is the single source of truth for now (stolen devices and recovery are out of scope). Owning an agent gives it nothing. What it may do comes only from policies on the identity it acts for, given by that identity: your phone gets act, own and govern on you; a coop's always-on server gets act on the coop only to carry one list. Act's one condition is data: a map from data ID to an ordinary Operations object (D56), conditions included: {"act": {"data": {"data:b3:7Hq…#house-list": {"want": {}, "keep": {}}}}}. Without data, act covers all of the owner's data. Agents are never in roles and never get data policies; data policies go to roles of humans and coops (D6, D44). A change or a read is allowed only if both layers allow it. A policy belongs to the identity that gave it, not to the agent that signed it; it ends only by that identity's ending or its expiry. The owner and its first agent are born together in one record. Acting for an identity is a chain of policies, one per hop: an agent acts for its owner; an identity acts for a coop through the coop's policy to a role that lists it; the chain is as long as needed (phone → you → home → street; home's server → home). Agent policies on an identity are written by that identity's guardian (D70).
decisions.why: Two clean layers: who speaks for an identity, and what an identity may do with data. The same two layers decide which keys an agent gets (D57).

decisions.title: One top: one owner per piece of data, one guardian per coop
decisions.decision: Authority has exactly one top and flows only downward. A piece of data has one owner (D5). A coop has one guardian: its govern policy goes to a guardian role that holds exactly one identity; its members role gets act and own, one signature each (D49). Nobody can give more than it holds, and nobody can remove the one above it. When two holders below the top remove each other at the same moment, both removals stand and the top repairs, for example by adding one back; there is no seniority and no coin flip. The top cannot clash with itself because it is one. A guardian hands govern on before stepping down. Signature counts for govern come later as condition plugins.
decisions.why: Without a total order, peers with equal power can remove each other at once and leave nobody, and with one signature any member could take a coop over. Keyhive's Keyline calls this mutual destruction in the root role; its mitigation is a single owner at the top, with every layer below repairable from above. Gnosis Safes avoid it with a blockchain's total order, which a local-first system does not have.

decisions.title: Only the owner ends policies; expiry is checked on every change
decisions.decision: Every change carries the time its author signed it and counts only if that time is before the expiry of the policy it relies on; devices reject times far ahead of their own clock. Only the owner's agents write endings into the history: a revoke at any time, a lapse once the date has passed. An ending drops only the ended holder's own changes that it did not list as seen (D61), never anyone else's. Policies expire after 30 days unless set otherwise; the owner renews unchanged policies a week before they end, and a renewal names the policy it renews, so ending one ends the chain. renew is its own operation, so a coop can give one always-on agent only that job. Other peers may stop handing out keys and chunks once a date has passed by their own clock: a local choice, never written into the history. An owner who is offline never causes a wipe. An ending turns the data key if the ended policy gave read, and is the delete trigger on honest devices.
decisions.why: If any reader could write a lapse, a fast clock would end policies early, and a lapse claiming to have seen nothing would drop weeks of everyone's work. Keyhive has no expiry for this reason; Willow checks each entry's own timestamp. We combine both: per-change time checks, and endings only from the owner.

decisions.title: Every record says what it had seen
decisions.decision: Every signed record carries after (the latest changes its author had seen of the data, of the policy set and of each identity in its proof) and seq (its signer's running number). “Saw it” means listed in after, directly or through what those records saw. A list counts only for its author's own authority: nobody can make another signer's ending disappear by leaving it out. Two different records with the same signer and seq prove the signer lied: both are invalid.
decisions.why: Endings, removals and “less authority wins” depend on what came before what; without it in the record, “never saw it” is undefined. Keyhive's revocations record the content heads their issuer had seen for the same reason.

decisions.title: History keeps everything; what you see is computed
decisions.decision: No change is ever removed from the sealed history. What you see is computed: the valid changes always form one causally complete version, which every device computes the same way and Loro can open. An ending invalidates the ended holder's own changes that it did not see, and with them every change built on them. Honest changes that fell only because they built on an invalid one come back to their authors as a conflict view, and their devices apply them again as new changes, as for late writers after a cut (D39). The next cut removes invalid changes for good.
decisions.why: An op-based CRDT cannot skip an operation: Loro keeps a change whose dependencies are missing as pending. Keyhive lists what happens to a revoked writer's content as an open question (whiteout).

decisions.title: One writer can't make devices disagree
decisions.decision: A change's Loro peer ID is derived from its agent, epoch and data ID (D69), so nobody can write under another's ID. Two different changes with the same peer and counter prove the signer lied: both are invalid and its policy is ended. On arrival, each change is checked on its own: signature, policy, the schema's shape. Rules that span concurrent changes (limits, required entries across a list, loops of coops inside coops) are settled when the view is built, in one fixed order (causal order, then hash). A change that uses an unknown plugin waits until the plugin is known; it is not rejected.
decisions.why: Otherwise one authorised writer could split devices for good: by signing two versions of one change, by two changes that are valid alone but not together, or by a plugin old devices don't know.

decisions.title: Data is named by the hash of its birth record
decisions.decision: A piece of data is born with a birth record: its schema, its first policy naming the owner (own, no expiry) and a random nonce, signed by an agent acting for the owner with own. The data ID is data:b3: and the BLAKE3 hash of the record without its signature. There is no seal: nothing has to be kept or destroyed, and a second birth record is simply different data. A proof starts at a birth record, whose ID names it. New data born inside another piece of data (an item of a list) is born under the parent's create policy and follows the parent's owner and policies by link.
decisions.why: A data ID that is a key's public half trusts the creator to destroy the key; one who keeps it can sign a second birth and become a second owner. Keyhive warns of the same: a retained subject key can re-root a document. Naming by hash is what D50 already does for identities.

decisions.title: Carriers see who may carry, never what is inside
decisions.decision: The policies, roles and endings of a piece of data are signed but not encrypted for the peers that carry it, with pseudonymous IDs; content and keyrings stay sealed. A carrier checks every want against them and learns endings, so it stops serving an ended holder. A want is signed over the carrier's fresh challenge, so it cannot be replayed elsewhere. Peers forward news and run set summaries only for data both sides may want. What a carrier learns is stated plainly: chunk hashes, sizes and links, the signing agents, who may carry and read the data (pseudonymously), and when it changes. A relay (D28) is different: it only forwards encrypted packets between two devices and holds nothing.
decisions.why: A carrier cannot check proofs against policies it cannot see, nor stop serving a revoked holder if endings are hidden from it. Keyhive's relays see the membership graph for the same reason and list it as unprotected metadata.

decisions.title: Schema versions are frozen and travel with the data
decisions.decision: Every piece of data names a schema version in its birth record; a Value's metadata Doc names one for the Value and one for itself. A schema is a JSON Schema edited as a Loro Doc with its own birth record, owner and policies. Each published version is frozen: its ID is the BLAKE3 hash of its canonical CBOR, and the frozen version is a Value carried with every piece of data that pins it, so no schema owner can take it away. Every change names the version it was written in and is checked against that version; a change naming a version or lens a device doesn't have yet waits. Paths (JSON Pointer, * for any index or key) give every part of the data an address for policies and operations. Every reference to a schema, a plugin's specification or input shape, or the registry of operation names is a data ID with @ and a version hash; never a bare name. The #label after it is only for people.
decisions.why: A live schema Doc read under its owner's policies would let that owner block every list that uses it, and a Loro state has no content hash to pin. Frozen, carried versions fix both.

decisions.title: Lenses between versions; moving on rewrites nothing
decisions.decision: A new version comes with a lens: a list of operations (rename, add with a default, remove with a value for old readers, copy, convert by registered two-way conversions, wrap, hoist) that runs both ways, is named by its hash and can be checked by anyone: applied to the old version it must give exactly the new one. Ambiguous lenses are refused. Each version maps its paths to stored keys; a rename keeps the stored key, an added field gets a new one, a removed field's key stays. The owner moves the data to a new version with one signed migration record (an ownership act, D30) that rewrites nothing; the data then accepts changes in every version along its lenses, until the owner retires one. Every device merges first, then projects the merged state along the lens path (shortest, ties to the smaller lens ID) into its own version. Policies and operations name the version their paths use; the data is projected into that version, and policies are never translated. Two concurrent migrations both stand until the owner writes a version with a lens from each.
decisions.why: Old and new apps keep working on the same data at the same time, with no flag day and nothing rewritten. Jazz 2 and Cambria show the shape; stored keys make it fit a CRDT, where Cambria's op-by-op translation on Automerge was abandoned.

decisions.title: Breaking changes go through a Loro branch
decisions.decision: A change that a lens cannot run both ways (splitting a field, a list becoming a map) is a rewrite. The owner's agent takes the frontier F of the valid view, forks the Doc at F (fork_at), applies the lens there and takes the diff; on the main Doc it checks out F, edits detached under its derived peer ID (D63), applies the diff and commits one change that depends on F, signed with a migration record. Ops made on the fork are never signed. Every peer verifies by repeating the rewrite at F; a mismatch is dropped. Old-version changes that never saw the rewrite go back to their authors, who apply them again through the lens (D62). A total break may instead start new data with its own birth record and end the old data's write policies.
decisions.why: Loro has no branch object, but fork_at, checkout and apply_diff give a deterministic branch-and-merge that every peer can recompute, so nobody has to trust the migrating device.

decisions.title: Joining by invite; agent epochs
decisions.decision: A new agent joins by invite. An agent with govern writes an invite record into the identity's history: a one-time public key, a short expiry and exactly the operations the new agent gets, within its own. The one-time secret goes to the new device out of band (QR code or typed code). The new device makes its own signer and lock and signs its birth record, which names the invite and carries a second signature by the one-time key. That pair is the new agent's policy, exactly as granted: no other agent has to be online. An invite is single use: two births citing it are both invalid; the owner may end an unused invite. Every agent record carries rev (signer revision) and epoch (continuity epoch); a restored or reinstalled device writes an epoch record and starts a new epoch, so it never reuses a running number or a CRDT op ID.
decisions.why: Pairing needs no second device online and can't be widened by the new device; a copied code is worthless after one use or its expiry. An honest restore no longer looks like a lying signer.

decisions.title: One guardian per identity, changed only by succession
decisions.decision: Every human and every coop has exactly one guardian, the one top of its authority, which alone holds govern on it. A human is its own guardian and acts as one through its own agents with govern (passkeys are the single source of truth for now). A coop's guardian is its guardian role, which always holds exactly one identity. A coop's guardian changes only by succession: the current guardian signs a new guardian role record naming its successor, which must list the previous one as seen. A guardian can't leave or be removed without naming a successor, so no coop ends up without one. If two guardian role records are concurrent (the guardian's own agents disagreed), neither takes effect until a record sees both. Agents have no guardian; their owner governs them. Below the guardian, concurrent removals both stand and the guardian repairs (D59). Several guardians acting by majority, with chained signatures, may come later. The guardian exercises govern through its own chain (your phone → you → the coop); a coop's own agents never hold govern on it.
decisions.why: Keeps one top, so no two equals can remove each other at once and a coop can never lock itself out, without signature counts or quorums yet. The word guardian says what the role is for: keeping the coop whole.

decisions.title: Successor records for data
decisions.decision: New data may name a predecessor in its birth record (data ID and frontier hash), and the old data gets a signed forward link from its owner. This is the path for total schema breaks and any future change of owner.
decisions.why: Data named by its birth record has no way to continue under a new one.

decisions.title: Values named by the hash of their ciphertext
decisions.decision: Sealed Values are stored and named by the BLAKE3 hash of their ciphertext; the plaintext hash appears only inside the sealed metadata Doc. Encryption runs in segments aligned to iroh-blobs' 16 KiB groups, so ranges stay decryptable.
decisions.why: Carriers can't check a plaintext hash, and the name lets anyone confirm that you hold a file they know.

decisions.title: Acknowledged finality and owner checkpoints
decisions.decision: Every record's after is an acknowledgement. Once every current reader, or the owner in a signed checkpoint, has acknowledged a frontier, it is final: nothing before it is evaluated again, cuts and compaction start there instead of at a clock age, and a record that claims to change the final past proves its signer lied.
decisions.why: Without finality, a late ending can unwind arbitrarily old changes built on the ended holder's.

decisions.title: Lens properties, version negotiation, retiring versions
decisions.decision: Every lens gets property tests in the shape of Jazz's INV-LENS-14 (translate then apply equals apply then translate). Versions that need no rewrite pass an additive-only check. Peers exchange the versions they speak at the start of sync. The owner retires a version with an ending.
decisions.why: Peers must carry every version in use, with no way to retire one, and nothing checks lenses beyond their shape.

decisions.title: Limits counted per author; no remote queries in iroh-blobs
decisions.decision: Limits such as “20 items” count along each author's own running number, so they are checked on arrival and never flip. iroh-blobs' Observe is disabled except for the owner's agents. Query results are cached per schema version.
decisions.why: A limit settled when the view is built can flip changes that were already accepted, and Observe is a remote query against D24.

decisions.title: Role deltas, invites, and writes imply read
decisions.decision: Role records become add and remove deltas; a removal beats a concurrent add of the same identity, and nothing else. A revoke beats a concurrent renewal of the same policy. The owner can sign invite records (“whoever presents this one-time key may join role R until T”), so joining needs no owner online. Create, update and delete on content require read; write-only comes later with write keys.
decisions.why: Full role lists lose unrelated concurrent adds, a revoke concurrent with a renewal is unspecified, every join needs the owner online, and a writer without the data key can't encrypt.

decisions.title: Signer hash chains; endings name chain heads
decisions.decision: Every signer's records form a hash chain (running number plus previous hash); chain headers travel without content. Every ending or removal names the ended signer's chain head, and records that are not ancestors of that head are dropped on all data. The owner, the one top, is the linearisation point for its own authority.
decisions.why: Critical: an ending in another history (an agent revoked on its human, a member removed from a coop) can't be listed by the data's records, so backdated changes slip in.

decisions.title: Lies freeze the signer; warrants
decisions.decision: Two records with one signer and one running number freeze that signer from the earliest lied-about number; a lie never voids an ending. A warrant (a signed record carrying both conflicting records) travels on the signer's identity topic; carriers check it and refuse the signer's chunks. p2panda's resolver cases become test fixtures.
decisions.why: As written, both conflicting records become invalid, which a signer could use to void a record it regrets.

decisions.title: Safe key turns
decisions.decision: A writer encrypts only under a key whose recipients are all among its current readers, otherwise it turns the key first. Among concurrent valid key turns the owner's agent's wins, otherwise the lowest (signer, running number). Key generations are named by a hash of the key turn, with the counter only as a hint. Every key turn is checked for envelope completeness. Chunk headers name the key generation, and the AEAD binds data ID, generation, signer and chunk hash.
decisions.why: Concurrent key turns fork, a counter can't tell them apart, and a turner that hasn't seen a removal leaks its key to the removed reader.

decisions.title: Forward-secure envelopes
decisions.decision: Agent locks become rotating signed pre-keys with a lifetime, published in the agent's history (as in X3DH). Each envelope also carries fresh key material for the next envelope to that recipient (2SM, from the DCGKA paper), so every lock key is used once.
decisions.why: Today a stolen agent lock opens every envelope ever sealed to it, meaning all past role keys.

decisions.title: An invalid add turns keys; envelopes after acknowledgement
decisions.decision: An add that ends up invalid (made by an agent whose policy was ended at the same moment) counts as a removal for keys: the keys it handed out turn. Newcomers receive envelopes only once their add is acknowledged by the owner's agents.
decisions.why: p2panda's leak case at the agent level: the add is dropped, but the newcomer already holds the keys and nothing turns them.

decisions.title: Endings that hold in time
decisions.decision: A change's signed time must be at least every time in its after and must never fall per signer. An always-on owner agent may only renew and lapse. Far-future records wait instead of being rejected for good. An ending is delivered to the ended agent, then its connections are closed, it is dropped as a neighbour and its transfers are aborted.
decisions.why: A holder can sign a time just before expiry and send it later; an owner away in the renewal week locks the household out; no iroh layer revokes anything.

decisions.title: Forgetting safely
decisions.decision: Back-links to older keys are deleted once every reader has acknowledged the newer generation. Values the live state no longer references are garbage-collected within retain rules. Wants and changes on QUIC 0-RTT streams are refused. A keep carrier signs a receipt for each stored chunk before any cut.
decisions.why: Back-links stay for 30 days whatever readers have done, and 0-RTT data can be replayed.

decisions.title: A separate network key; no open gossip
decisions.decision: Each agent gets a network key separate from its signer, certified in its history (“endpoint E acts for agent A until T”) and rotatable on its own. We run our own relay, whose access callback runs theOS checks; address lookup is filled from directory records; mDNS advertising is off or renamed. Gossip topics are replaced by direct subscriptions after a want check; any remaining topic is a keyed hash of data ID and key generation.
decisions.why: iroh needs the raw secret in memory and hands it out, so the signer can't live in an HSM; relays and lookups link every conversation to one ID; iroh-gossip lets anyone who knows a topic join, watch and inject news.

decisions.title: Chunk commitments and policy-first sync
decisions.decision: Each chunk header carries a signed Merkle root over that signer's chunks for the data, so carriers can check gaps and lies without keys. Peers exchange policy, role and ending heads before chunks, and forward warrant pairs first. iroh-blobs moves the bytes behind its request intercept; fingerprints and summaries run on our own ALPN.
decisions.why: A merged chunk can leave a change out unnoticed, and peers build on changes they will drop later.

decisions.title: Connection-bound wants and carrier freshness
decisions.decision: A want is the signer's signature over the connection's exported keying material (label theos/want/1, context the data ID): fresh, bound to the connection, no extra round trip. Records a carrier sees use per-data pseudonyms. A carrier serves only while its newest record from the owner is younger than its own policy's lifetime. Each piece of data lives on at least two carriers from different operators, with quotas and priorities as conditions on keep.
decisions.why: Stable IDs let a carrier link a person across data; a carrier that hasn't heard an ending keeps serving.

decisions.title: Ending events and two ways to drop
decisions.decision: For every ending the engine emits the IDs of the changes it invalidates, so apps can show moderation and the conflict view. A schema says how its data drops invalid changes: replayed without them (text, D62) or removed by ID (messages, posts); both converge.
decisions.why: Apps would otherwise recompute what an ending removed, and replaying is costly for simple append-only data.

decisions.title: One ordering pipeline; delivery apart from processing
decisions.decision: One buffer orders every record kind (policies, endings, key turns, changes) and releases each once its dependencies are in; a logical depth next to the hashes makes concurrency checks cheap. Checking, ordering, decrypting and applying form one pipeline; delivery is pluggable: iroh, carriers, LAN broadcast, or a sealed bundle on a USB stick.
decisions.why: Today each record kind waits in its own way, and delivery is tied to iroh.

decisions.title: A message mode with forward secrecy, later
decisions.decision: Alongside data keys, where a newcomer may read history, a second mode for chat-like data uses a fresh key per message (a Double Ratchet over the same key agreement), chosen per piece of data.
decisions.why: Data keys give no forward secrecy for content; chats may want it.

decisions.title: Records follow schemas too; a root manifest with the meta-schema
decisions.decision: A record's type is a schema ref (data ID @ version), never a name. Each engine release carries one root manifest: the meta-schema (JSON Schema 2020-12 plus theOS's vocabulary for stored keys and lenses) and one schema version per record kind. The engine trusts exactly those hashes. The meta-schema validates itself, and every schema version, root or not, validates against it. A record whose type isn't in the device's manifest, or reachable from it through lenses, waits. A new manifest keeps old record versions readable through lenses; records are never rewritten.
decisions.why: The rule “refer to schemas by data ID and version, never by name” must hold for records too, and something has to check the first schema: a fixed, hash-named root set with a self-validating meta-schema closes the loop.
